title: Ben Maher wins Spruce Meadows grand prix in Grand Slam showdown
content:
There are few harsher agonies than waiting, and throughout the great expanse of the CPKC ‘International’ Grand Prix presented by Rolex at the Spruce Meadows ‘Masters’, two riders felt that in very different ways.

Germany’s Richard Vogel endured hours of waiting in pursuit of the final leg of the Rolex Grand Slam. He waited through two and a half hours of first-round riders, another hour or so of second-round riders, and a final half an hour of jump-off rounds, of which his would be the sixth and final.

Britain’s Ben Maher was enduring the literal agony of a shoulder injury, sustained in a fall in Saturday’s Nations Cup class, which left the rider with a limited range of motion as he waited to close out the competition.

Vogel was the favorite, both for show jumping fans and by the statistics sheet. Could Vogel become just the second-ever rider to win this Grand Slam and scoop $1.2 million (€1 million) bonus?

The question for Maher was whether he could ride at all on Sunday.

He very nearly didn’t.

“It was a very long night, and I was very close to not riding today. But I persevered and dug in,” Maher said.

In the first round, despite visibly favouring his right arm, he and the twelve-year-old Enjou de Grisien knocked a single rail over. Course designer Leopoldo Palacios’s influential track featured a rollback to the water tray — a bit of trickery that Palacios had famously used at the 2000 Sydney Olympics and had shelved since. The rail very nearly put Maher out of contention. Just twelve of the starting 40 would qualify for round two, and there had been seven clears, one of which was Vogel’s. But that one-rail round was swift enough, and they returned — on the back foot, perhaps, but still in the hunt.

In the second round, though, none of the seven who had jumped clear previously managed to do so a second time. Two of the first-round four-faulters, for their part, were clear on the second attempt. Had any rider kept a clean sheet — as the United States’ Lillie Keenan and Fasther so nearly did — the competition would have ended there. Instead, six riders carrying a two-phase score of four faults for a single rail down apiece proceeded to a jump-off finale.

Switzerland’s Steve Guerdat, the newly-crowned World Champion, set an early precedent, lodging a clear round in a time of 42.25 with the relatively inexperienced Albfuehren’s Iashin Sitte. Maher followed him into the ring and gritted his teeth through a series of tight rollback turns, requiring upper-body strength, to also deliver a clear and shave 0.85 seconds off of Guerdat’s time.

Vogel, riding United Touch S, was next.

The pair are masters of jump-offs. The stallion’s freakishly long stride pattern allows him to ride fewer steps between fences and the pair’s ineffable balance has seen them produce rollback turns that shouldn’t even be possible. Over the first and second fences they were on song. To the third, they produced one of those Vogel-exclusive turns, gaining a valuable half-second on the clock in doing so. Then, galvanised, they turned back to a double combination.

Nothing quite went wrong — not in the way it had last month, for example, when they stopped at the base of a fence in the individual final at the World Championships. But in top-level show jumping, there is no room for anything less than perfect. They did not have that final 5%; instead, they took the top rail from its cups. The Grand Slam dream was over. Vogel and United Touch S finished fifth.

Just Keenan could usurp Maher, and after a furtive hug of her horse’s neck before the starting bell, the 29-year-old certainly tried. But although she and Fasther left every fence up, and ate up the distance to the final fence, they were 0.45 seconds short of Maher’s time. She would settle for second and Guerdat third. Maher, on his 28th attempt, would finally lift a Rolex Grand Slam leg trophy.

“It’s starting to sink in, and it’s incredible to win one of these Majors and what we all consider one of the biggest, if not the biggest, Grand Prix in the world,” said Maher. “I’ve been coming here for many, many years, and I really felt this year that Enjeu had a chance.”

Enjeu de Grisien and Maher had come so close at Aachen Masters.

“We finished fourth, and was just kind of knocking on the door,” Maher said. “It’s been a bit like that for the last two years, actually, but we have to keep picking ourselves up.”

Not least, of course, when literally meeting the ground, as Maher did with Catelly in Saturday’s Nations Cup. Though the horse was uninjured, Maher’s hard landing recalls a similar incident in 2023 when a shoulder fracture and dislocation forced him to undergo extensive surgery and miss the first four months of that season.

The Rolex trophy, and the richest prize purse in equestrian sport, will be some consolation as he and his team assess the damage.

“I’m getting too old for that,” Maher said. “I haven’t had many falls, but it seems that when I do, lately, they’re bad. We did some tests today and I was able to hold Enjeu. He’s a game horse, and I knew he’d be pulling a bit today because he’d be excited. But it was all manageable — it was just getting on and off him that was a bit sensitive. I had a lot of talks with my doctors and physio and my family this morning, and I’m just glad I made the right decision.”

Maher now becomes the live contender in the Rolex Grand Slam, and will have a chance to fight for a second win at Switzerland’s CHI Geneva in December.

“These are tough competitions to win, but these Majors are the pinnacle of our sport. They’re what everyone wants to win and why we keep trying. I’ve been close a few times and never managed to do it – maybe this has changed the dark omen that’s been following me for a few years and I can just enjoy the ride now.”
